title: More Canadians are using cannabis daily than are drinking alcohol daily: study
summary: Daily use of cannabis has outstripped daily use of alcohol in Canada, with young Canadians at the front of the trend, new data shows. Experts say this generational shift brings some positives, but…

image.caption: The number of Canadians reporting daily cannabis use is now higher than the number reporting daily alcohol consumption, a new study published Monday has found. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Daily use of cannabis has outstripped daily use of alcohol in Canada, according to a new study, with young Canadians as the main driver — signalling a shift in our habits that experts say has far-reaching implications.

A study published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ) analyzed survey data from nearly 100,000 Canadians and found that 5.7 per cent of people — roughly 1.8 million Canadians — reported using cannabis every day or nearly every day, compared to 5.2 per cent who reported daily or near daily alcohol use.
Only Canadians over 50 still reported higher rates of daily alcohol use compared to daily cannabis use.

"What we're kind of seeing is this generational shift between these different substances," said André McDonald, a postdoctoral fellow at the Peter Boris Centre for Addictions Research at McMaster University in Hamilton and lead author of the study.
"Historically, a lot of public health has focused on cigarette use and alcohol use. But these findings are kind of suggesting that we have to take daily cannabis use pretty seriously."
Researchers looked at the nationally representative 2023 to 2024 Canadian Community Health Survey to measure patterns of daily use of alcohol, cigarettes and cannabis.

When taking all age groups into consideration, the daily rate of cigarette use was the highest of the three at 8.5 per cent. But among adults younger than 35 years old, daily cannabis use was not only higher than daily alcohol use, but also higher than daily cigarette use.

Men aged 25-34 had the highest rate of daily cannabis use of any age group, at nearly 11 per cent. The percentage of women aged 18-24 who reported daily cannabis use was more than 17 times higher than the percentage that reported daily alcohol use.

It's part of an apparent cultural shift that extends beyond Canada. In the U.S., where many states now permit legal or medicinal cannabis, studies have shown that cannabis is outpacing alcohol as the daily drug of choice, with one 2024 study finding that 17.7 million people used cannabis daily or near-daily in the U.S. compared to 14.7 million daily or near-daily drinkers.

A person walks by a cannabis dispensary on Queen Street in Toronto. Among Canadians under 35, the number reporting they used cannabis every day was higher than those reporting they smoked cigarettes or drank alcohol every day. (Cole Burston/The Canadian Press)
Public messaging needs to keep up by apprising Canadians of the risks that come with heavy use, McDonald said.

"If, [for] the younger generations, this is becoming their preference, we could see this becoming a long-term trend," McDonald said. "It's very possible that … as they become older, these patterns are going to become middle-aged patterns."

Researchers noted that the study is limited by its use of self-reported data and the fact that the survey didn't look at how many times a day Canadians were using these substances if they reported daily use. It also did not include vaping.
Positive signs in drop of daily alcohol, tobacco

Does this study mean more and more Canadians are lighting up a joint every day as time goes on? Not necessarily — the survey is a snapshot of habits in 2023-2024, meaning the data doesn't show exactly when daily cannabis use overtook daily alcohol use.
About 41 per cent of those who reported daily or near daily cannabis use in the study said they started using cannabis daily after legalization in 2018.

blocks.text: "For cannabis, we saw a bump in the first year or two after legalization and then it's actually flattened — so it's a question of alcohol and smoking tobacco coming down more so than cannabis going up," said David Hammond, a professor in the School of Public Health Sciences at the University of Waterloo, who studies tobacco and cannabis harm reduction and was not involved in the study.

In Canada, the smoking of cigarettes has been declining for decades due to public health campaigning to highlight the serious cancer and health risks. Drinking has also been going down, with recent studies and polls highlighting that younger generations are drinking less than previous generations.
New report shows British Columbians are drinking less alcohol
The shift has some positive indications for public health in Canada.

Broadly speaking, daily cannabis use isn't associated with nearly as many negative health outcomes as daily alcohol and cigarette use is, Hammond said, and certainly not the "same levels of mortality."

blocks.text: "About half of all long-term tobacco smokers will die, and alcohol has a range of direct health effects [including] impaired driving and social disorders, so it's actually not much of a competition. Alcohol and tobacco take the trophy in terms of the biggest harms among Canadians."
But while cannabis is seen as a much safer drug in general, health experts caution that the occasional partaking of cannabis products is very different from heavy use — and that there are risks.
The dangers of overuse of cannabis

We don't have as much research on the long-term impacts of cannabis compared to alcohol and cigarettes. But there's strong evidence that too much cannabis use, particularly among young people, can lead to addiction and have serious mental health implications, said Romina Mizrahi, a psychiatrist and director of the McGill Research Centre for Cannabis in Montreal.
For those over 25, the concerns with daily use are largely "changes in their mood and their motivation," she told CBC News.

blocks.text: But for those in their teens and early twenties, overuse of cannabis can increase their risk of psychosis, something Mizrahi said most patients aren't aware of. The risk grows when more potent, high-THC cannabis products are involved.
Apart from age, the study found that income was also connected to high rates of daily cannabis use.
As high-potency THC demand grows, experts call for more research on cannabis compounds

The less money Canadians made, the more likely they were to report daily cannabis use, while Canadians in the highest income bracket (making more than $150,000 per year) reported the lowest rates of daily cannabis use.
Other groups that reported high rates of daily cannabis use included transgender and gender-diverse Canadians, as well as people with mood or anxiety disorders.

blocks.text: Those experiencing the stress that comes with marginalization or income pressures may be more likely to lean on cannabis to deal with it, McDonald said.
But with overuse, what can start out as a treatment for anxiety can end up perpetuating or exacerbating it, Mizrahi said.

"People tend to start using because they feel it can help them with their anxiety and even their mood sometimes. And what happens is when it becomes a regular use, then their anxiety levels start to creep up, and the same with depression and mood symptoms."

The rotating set of health warnings on cannabis products intended for smoking does include a warning that "cannabis can cause psychotic symptoms like severe paranoia," and that this risk is greater in those younger than 25.
But experts say that as Canadians' habits shift, we may need stronger visual warnings, like those on cigarette packaging, and more awareness so that Canadians can make informed choices.
Researchers suggest link between cannabis use and rise in psychotic disorder diagnoses
"The more we talk about this, especially for young people, the more they're going to be aware of it, and maybe they are going to reduce their use," Mizrahi said.
"Daily use is a problem. Daily use is a problem for alcohol, daily use is a problem for tobacco, obviously, and it is a problem for cannabis."
